title: 2011 AMC 12A Problem 22
statement: Let \(R\) be a square region and \(n \ge 4\) an integer. A point \(X\) in the interior of \(R\) is called \(n\)-ray partitional if there are \(n\) rays emanating from \(X\) that divide \(R\) into \(n\) triangles of equal area. How many points are \(100\)-ray partitional but not \(60\)-ray partitional?

solutions.text:
Scale the square to \([0,1]^2\) and write \(X=(x,y).\) The rays must include those through the four vertices. Every small triangle has area \(\frac{1}{n}.\) The triangles whose bases partition the bottom side together have area \(\frac{y}{2},\) so their number is \(\frac{ny}{2}.\) Similarly, the numbers along the top, left, and right sides are \(\frac{n(1-y)}{2},\) \(\frac{nx}{2},\) and \(\frac{n(1-x)}{2}.\)

These four numbers must be positive integers. Hence \(n\) is even and \[ \begin{gathered} X=\left(\dfrac{2i}{n},\dfrac{2j}{n}\right), \\ 1\le i,j\le\dfrac n2-1. \end{gathered} \] Conversely, partitioning each side into the indicated number of equal segments and joining the division points to \(X\) produces \(n\) equal-area triangles. Thus these are exactly the partitional points.

For \(n=100,\) the points are \((\frac{i}{50},\frac{j}{50})\) with \(1\le i,j\le49,\) giving \(49^2=2401.\) Such a point is also \(60\)-ray partitional exactly when \(\frac{i}{50}=\frac{c}{30}\) and \(\frac{j}{50}=\frac{d}{30}\) for integers \(c,d.\) Thus \(i\) and \(j\) must both be multiples of \(5.\) There are \(9\) choices for each, so the overlap has \(9^2=81\) points.

So the count is \(2401 - 81 = 2320.\)

Thus, the correct answer is C.
hints: The \(n\)-ray partitional points form a grid: for \(n = 2m,\) they are the interior points \(\left(\tfrac{i}{m}, \tfrac{j}{m}\right),\) an \((m-1) \times (m-1)\) array
A point is both \(100\)- and \(60\)-ray partitional exactly when it is \(20\)-ray partitional
